q: Do the Brown-Eastin block-eigenvalue formulas continue to match Stim RB fits at n=3 and n=4 qubits, where block-size asymmetry (4^n+2^n)/2 vs (4^n-2^n)/2 becomes significantly larger and the multi-exponential structure should be more visible under mildly asymmetric noise?
basis: Present replication covers only n=2. Paper's formulas scale to arbitrary n but were derived analytically without numerical support at any n. Higher n is the natural stress test for both the block decomposition and mixing-time behavior of the random-walk subgroup sampler.
next_steps: Extend rb_replication.py to n in {3,4} using Stim's tableau backend (still tractable — RB circuits are stabilizer). Sweep symmetric depolarizing p_dep in {0.001, 0.005, 0.01} and asymmetric single-Pauli-axis noise. Report fit lambda vs theory for real-Clifford lambda_1 and CNOT+Pauli lambda_1..lambda_4. Check whether walk_len=60 remains sufficient at larger n by measuring the empirical mixing (compare fitted lambda across walk_len in {30,60,120,240}).

q: How does the framework extend to hardware-native gate sets that are proper subgroups of Clifford but distinct from the two subgroups covered in the paper — specifically the neutral-atom Rydberg CZ + single-qubit-rotation set, and the ion-trap Molmer-Sorensen XX(theta=pi/2) + single-qubit-Clifford set?
basis: The paper's proof strategy (twirl decomposition into Pauli-orbit blocks) is generic to any Clifford subgroup containing the Paulis. Rydberg CZ generates the CNOT+Pauli subgroup up to basis change (already covered), but the MS-XX set may generate a genuinely different subgroup with different block structure. Practical RB on these platforms is currently done with software-compiled Clifford sequences that hide gate-set restriction; native-set RB would give a more honest error rate.
next_steps: Enumerate the Pauli-orbit blocks for {H, S, MS_XX(pi/2)} and for {global R_x(pi/2), CZ_ij, individual Pauli-Z} by brute-force character-table computation for n=2,3 (subgroup order small enough to enumerate). Then run Stim-based RB from |0..0> and |+..+> and check whether the observed decay matches the enumerated block eigenvalues. Publish a table of native-set block structures usable by experimentalists.

q: Can a character-RB variant (Helsen et al. 2019, 2022) be layered on top of the Brown-Eastin block structure to independently resolve individual block eigenvalues lambda_1..lambda_k from a single set of RB sequences, instead of requiring one distinct initial-state experiment per block?
basis: Standard RB from a single initial state extracts only one lambda per experiment (the one corresponding to the block whose projector has non-zero overlap with rho_0). Character-RB uses group-theoretic characters to weight measurement outcomes so that each character projects out a single block. Brown-Eastin block decomposition is exactly the input character-RB needs, but the paper does not discuss this combination.
next_steps: Compute the irreducible characters of the real-Clifford subgroup and CNOT+Pauli subgroup on n=2 qubits (finite group, tractable). Implement character-weighted survival estimator in the Stim harness. Verify on the pure-Z-noise asymmetric case that a single |00> experiment with character weighting recovers both lambda_1=1 and lambda_2=0.9472 without needing the |++> re-run. Compare sample efficiency vs the two-initial-state protocol.

q: How does an ML-boosted decay-fit estimator (e.g. gradient-boosted or transformer-based sequence-to-lambda regressor trained on synthetic Stim runs) perform on the Brown-Eastin subgroup RB curves compared to non-linear least squares on the exponential model, particularly in the low-sequence-count regime (N_seq < 30) where the paper's bounds become loose?
basis: Non-linear least squares on f(m) = A*lambda^m + B is the field-standard fit but is noise-sensitive at short sequences and when B is degenerate with baseline. Recent RB literature (Youssry et al. 2024; Google Quantum AI benchmarking papers) shows ML fits can extract lambda with 2-3x lower variance from small samples by learning the joint distribution of (survival, m) rather than fitting a mean.
next_steps: Generate 10k synthetic Stim RB runs across (subgroup, noise model, n) grid; train a small MLP/xgboost regressor to predict lambda from (m_i, survival_i, N_seq). Compare RMSE(fit, theory) at N_seq in {10, 30, 60, 100} against NLSQ. Free tools only: sklearn on the local m1 box. If ML wins, publish the trained estimator so experimentalists can extract subgroup-RB lambdas from smaller runs on real hardware.

q: Under coherent (non-Pauli) errors — specifically small over-rotation R_z(theta) with theta in {0.01, 0.05, 0.1} rad applied gate-independently — do the Brown-Eastin block eigenvalue formulas remain approximate predictors, or does the twirled channel acquire off-diagonal (block-mixing) contributions that make the multi-exponential model qualitatively fail?
basis: The paper assumes gate-independent Pauli noise; coherent errors are explicitly out of scope. But real hardware errors are ~50% coherent, and coherent errors do not commute cleanly with the Pauli-basis twirl. Standard Clifford RB is known to twirl coherent errors down to their Pauli approximation with a correction O(theta^2) — but this uses the full 2-design property which the restricted gate sets lack. The subgroups may not sufficiently twirl coherent errors, invalidating the closed forms.
next_steps: Extend rb_asym.py with a coherent-noise channel using Stim's noisy_unitary or a small density-matrix simulator (Qiskit statevector for n=2, still tractable). Sweep theta in {0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5} rad. Fit lambda_1, lambda_2 from |00>/|++> and check (a) whether the fit residual remains small (indicating still-exponential decay) and (b) whether extracted lambda tracks the effective p_Pauli = sin^2(theta/2) prediction. If block mixing occurs, quantify the second-exponential amplitude vs theta.
